column5: Arabic خ س ر / Aramaic חסר, table sound correspondence only
column6: The king is weighed in the balances and found deficient; the table's Aramaic lacking root joins a literal scale to the commentary's moral shortfall, though cognacy remains unverified.

column5: Numbered kingdom brought to an end
column6: Daniel explains that God has numbered the king's days and ended his rule; the counted time immediately precedes the short weight in the next verse.

column5: Silver weighers and traders cut off
column6: The inhabitants are told to wail because traders are destroyed and those weighing out silver are cut off; market, balance, and final closure meet in one announcement.

column5: Buyer and seller at the approaching day
column6: When the time and day arrive, neither buyer should rejoice nor seller mourn because judgment falls on all; the ordinary logic of a profitable transaction is suspended.
Silver is thrown into the streets and gold cannot deliver on the day of wrath or satisfy hunger; the commentary's capital has no use when its trading day ends.
God comes as a witness against those who defraud hired workers of wages and wrong vulnerable people; the commentary's due wage is a matter for final judgment.

column5: Integrity weighed on an honest scale
column6: Job asks to be weighed in a just balance so God may know his integrity; the commentary's market scale becomes a test of the person rather than the goods.

column5: Do not withhold good that is due
column6: The addressee must not withhold good from those to whom it is due when able to act; it states the commentary's mutual right as an immediate obligation.

column5: Do not defer payment until tomorrow
column6: One must not tell a neighbor to return tomorrow when the goods are in hand today; the owed portion has a deadline before time runs out.

column5: Do not exploit a needy hired worker
column6: The rule forbids oppression of poor hired workers, including resident foreigners; it identifies who is vulnerable before the same-day wage rule in the next verse.
The mortal heaps up wealth without knowing who will gather it; this precisely unsettles the commentary's hoarder who expects his capital to outlast his own time.
The speaker says God has made his days a few handbreadths and his lifetime nothing by comparison; time itself is a small measured holding.

column5: Workers enjoy the work of their hands
column6: People will build and inhabit and plant and eat, with days like a tree's; this reverses labor lost to another and gives the commentary's wage a durable setting.
The promised people will not labor in vain or bear children for calamity; enduring work and preserved family answer both forms of loss developed in the commentary.

column5: Reaper receives wage for eternal harvest
column6: The reaper already receives wages and gathers fruit for eternal life; the commentary's daily worker and final, lasting payment are joined explicitly.
The master says the idle servant should have placed his money with bankers so it returned with interest; merely preserving the principal fails the investment test.

column5: Stored goods imagined to buy many years
column6: The rich man addresses his soul as having goods stored for many years and plans to rest; it states the precise illusion about wealth and lengthened life corrected in the following verse.
The earth's merchants mourn because no one buys their cargo anymore; the commentary's open market ends without another buyer.
The lament says great wealth is laid waste in a single hour; it compresses the commentary's continuing capital loss into a final moment.

Paul distinguishes a worker's pay credited as an obligation from a gift credited by grace; this tests the commentary's moral wage metaphor against an explicit refusal to make divine credit ordinary wages.
Paul says the one who does not work but trusts God is credited with righteousness; the passage presses against reading belief and good work as jointly earning the payment.

column5: Gift produces credit in the giver's account
column6: Paul says he seeks fruit increasing to the donors' account rather than the gift itself; generosity becomes an accumulating return in the commentary's moral ledger.

column5: Lost property and better lasting possession
column6: The audience accepted the plunder of its goods because it knew it had a better and enduring possession; material principal can be lost without final loss.
Paul says his work showed the need to help the weak and recalls that giving is more blessed than receiving; earned goods become another's benefit.

column5: Worldly gain cannot compensate a soul
column6: Jesus asks what profit gaining the world has if one forfeits life and what could be given in exchange; it repeats the commentary's ultimate calculation of self-loss in another Gospel setting.
The Son of Man will come in glory and repay each person according to what each has done; the self-loss question in the preceding verse is followed by the work account.

column5: Agreed denarius for a day's work
column6: The vineyard owner agrees with laborers on a denarius for the day before sending them out; it sets the contracted amount whose evening distribution drives the story.
The owner still finds idle workers at the eleventh hour and asks why they stand there; meaningful work remains possible just before the daily deadline.
Jesus asks who will give the stewards their own if they have not been faithful with someone else's; entrusted capital is the test for lasting possession.
The person faithful in very little is faithful in much; the commentary's trust in dealings applies to small transactions before a greater settlement.

column5: Calculate loss of a good deed against reward
column6: The saying instructs a person to reckon a commandment's apparent loss against its reward and a transgression's apparent gain against its loss; it articulates the commentary's moral profit calculation.
The borrower is told not to forget a guarantor who has given his life for him; the source's secondary sabir as guarantor becomes a concrete and costly interpersonal obligation.
Jacob has Esau swear and Esau sells his birthright; a lasting share is exchanged for immediate consumption, making a disastrous trade of one's due portion.
Esau eats and drinks, leaves, and is said to have despised the birthright; the scene shows the short appetite behind the preceding loss of a lasting right.

column5: Esau's bargain read as moral warning
column6: Hebrews recalls Esau selling his birthright for a single meal to warn against an unholy choice; it interprets Genesis's market exchange as sacrificing a durable inheritance.
Hebrews says Esau later wanted the blessing but was rejected despite seeking it with tears; its reading of the birthright story meets the commentary's too-late plea for an extension.

column5: Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ and Arabic ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח, table sound correspondences only
column6: Jehoshaphat tells the people to believe the Lord and be established, and believe his prophets and succeed; the verse puts two table roots in sequence, linking trust to a prospering outcome without proving either cognacy.

column5: Arabic خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
column6: The righteous eats to satisfaction while the wicked person's stomach lacks; the Hebrew deficiency verb marks a concrete moral shortfall rather than a mere sad feeling.

column5: Life as a hired worker's term
column6: Job compares human days on earth to the days of a hired worker; it frames the wage longing in the next verse as a figure for mortal duration.
The wicked borrow and do not repay, while the righteous are generous and give; the commentary's mutual right is tested at the point of an outstanding debt.
The speaker commands rescue of people being taken to death; the next verse's divine weighing and repayment rests on this concrete neglected duty.
The prophet recalls a period with no wages for human or beast and no peace for travel; the absence of pay makes the coming restoration more than abstract prosperity.
The speaker's flesh and heart may fail, yet God remains his portion forever; the lasting share is opposed to the exhausted mortal self and goods.
The people are promised light if they pour themselves out for the hungry and satisfy the afflicted; the commentary's expiring personal capital is put to another's need.
The proverb calls a just balance and scales the Lord's and treats the weights as his work; fair commercial measurement belongs within divine order.
The prophet identifies wicked wealth and a deficient grain measure in the house; hoarded capital and short measure share one household.
The instruction says to remember that death will not delay; it counters the commentary's hope that a short extension will remain available.

column5: Give to a friend before death
column6: The speaker urges doing good to a friend and giving while still alive; possession can meet another's claim only before the human deadline.
Tobit tells his son almsgiving delivers from death and prevents descent into darkness; the stored treasure in the prior instruction has a concrete life-saving return.

column5: Little with righteousness exceeds unjust wealth
column6: Raphael ranks prayer and almsgiving with righteousness above riches with injustice; the scale of moral value differs from the amount in a purse.

column5: The grave does not cancel accounting
column6: The saying warns that death cannot serve as a refuge because one must give an account before the divine king; the commentary's closing day still leaves an audit.
The addressees must not store treasure where moth and rust destroy and thieves break in; this specifies how the commentary's earthly capital can disappear.

column5: Sell holdings and give poor for heavenly treasure
column6: Jesus tells a wealthy man to sell his possessions and give to the poor to have treasure in heaven; another person's need converts current capital into enduring value.

column5: Salvation described as grace through faith
column6: The letter says salvation comes by grace through faith as God's gift; it puts a gift frame beside the commentary's wage frame for believing.

column5: Not from works, so no boasting
column6: The writer explicitly excludes works as the source of salvation; this differs from any reading of the commentary's good-work wage as earned entitlement.

column5: Good works still prepared for believers
column6: The saved are described as created for good works in which to walk; it qualifies the previous gift language with a continuing place for intentional deeds.
James says Abraham's faith was active with his works and brought to completion through them; it develops the conjunction of believing and acting beyond the bare formula.
James concludes that a person is justified by works and not faith alone; it places the commentary's joined belief and work within a specific interpretive dispute.

column5: Sparing or generous sowing and reaping
column6: The measure of what one sows determines the harvest in Paul's appeal for a collection; charity is treated as an investment whose return follows its measure.
Paul says current abundance should supply others' lack and later the relationship may reverse, creating equality; the commentary's mutual rights are an exchange across time.
Paul asks what his wage is and answers that he preaches without charge rather than using his right in the gospel; refusing immediate pay itself becomes his chosen return.
The speaker says he searches minds and hearts and will give each according to works; intentional acts and the final payout are assessed together.
The one who conquers and keeps the speaker's works until the end receives authority; the reward requires continuing good action across the remaining time.
The scorching sun withers a flower, and the rich person similarly fades while pursuing business; time erodes both the trader and the expected gain.

column5: Unknown day and hour require watch
column6: The parable closes by telling hearers to watch because the day and hour are unknown; the closed door has an unknowable rather than negotiable deadline.
The teaching asks believers who share in immortal things to share even more in mortal goods and not claim these as solely their own; the commentary's passing capital carries a mutual obligation.
